name: Huachipaeri
confidence_why: Peck (1979 [1958]), the only first-hand phonology of Huachipaeri (Toyeri and Sapiteri dialects), puts stress on the penultimate syllable with an antepenultimate exception class and lengthened stressed vowels, in line with Van linden (2023) on the sister dialect Arakmbut, but he calls stress unresolved and reports an unpublished analysis by Pittman of Huachipaeri proper in which stress is non-phonemic and predictable from vowel length.

new_statements.quote: VII.A. ACENTO. En la mayoría de las palabras que tienen dos o más sílabas el acento se encuentra en la penúltima sílaba. Las excepciones son palabras que terminan con ciertas sílabas, tales como (-ta), (-nda) o (-na), (ne), (-a), et al., en las cuales se pone el acento sobre la antepenúltima sílaba. En aisladas respuestas pedidas con los sufijos arriba se han observado algunas variaciones en la colocación del acento. En verbos con una serie de sufijos, la colocación del acento y de la duración de la vocal es más compleja; puede resultar que los sufijos sean clíticos. El Señor Pittman, en su análisis no publicado de Huachipaeri, concluyó que se podía predecir el acento a base de las duraciones de vocales. (p. 27)
new_statements.translation: VII.A. STRESS. In most words of two or more syllables the stress falls on the penultimate syllable. The exceptions are words ending in certain syllables, such as (-ta), (-nda) or (-na), (ne), (-a), et al., in which the stress is placed on the antepenultimate syllable. In isolated elicited responses with the suffixes above some variation in the placement of stress has been observed. In verbs with a series of suffixes, the placement of stress and of vowel length is more complex; it may turn out that the suffixes are clitics. Mr. Pittman, in his unpublished analysis of Huachipaeri, concluded that stress could be predicted on the basis of vowel durations. (p. 27) — Also p. 12 (IV.H): 'El acento cae sobre la penúltima sílaba de la mayoría de las palabras, y está escrito solamente cuando se encuentra sobre otras sílabas.' = 'Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of most words, and is written only when it falls on other syllables'; fn. 3: 'El señor Pittman encontró en su análisis no publicado del idioma Huachipaeri que la duración de una vocal es fonémica, y que el acento es no-fonémico.' = 'Mr. Pittman found in his unpublished analysis of the Huachipaeri language that vowel length is phonemic and that stress is non-phonemic.' Fn. 2, p. 2: 'El acento está en la penúltima sílaba a menos que se indique de otra manera.' = 'Stress is on the penultimate syllable unless otherwise indicated.' Sec. VII.B, pp. 27-28: 'Todas las vocales acentuadas son prolongadas. ... No hemos encontrado pares mínimos de acento o de duración de vocales' = 'All stressed vowels are lengthened. ... We have found no minimal pairs for stress or for vowel length.'

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog holds Huachipaeri with an empty rule and there are no existing statements, so Peck supplies the placement: penultimate default with an antepenultimate exception class, stress correlated with vowel length, and a reported view (Pittman, unpublished) that in Huachipaeri proper stress is non-phonemic and predictable from vowel length. Data are from the Toyeri and Sapiteri dialects (see the note on which variety), not Huachipaeri proper, except the Pittman footnote.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress on the penultimate syllable in most words of two or more syllables; words ending in certain syllables (-ta, -nda, -na, -ne, -a, etc.) take antepenultimate stress instead; placement in long suffixed verbs is more complex (suffixes possibly clitics). All stressed vowels are lengthened; no minimal pairs for stress or length found. Peck lists stress, vowel length and morpheme boundary as 'unresolved' items (p. 2). Pittman's unpublished analysis of Huachipaeri proper (as reported by Peck) treats vowel length as phonemic and stress as non-phonemic, predictable from vowel durations.
new_statements.exceptions: Words ending in the syllables (-ta), (-nda) or (-na), (ne), (-a), 'et al.' take antepenultimate stress; some variation observed in isolated elicited forms with these suffixes; verbs with a series of suffixes have more complex stress and length placement (suffixes may be clitics); some morpheme boundaries affect stress (p. 12). Peck also notes the language is often spoken on a single pitch with a sudden drop near the end of the utterance (p. 12), i.e. no lexical tone.
new_statements.identity_note: Peck's data are from Toyeri (Madre de Dios river near the Inambari mouth, 1956-57) and Sapiteri (Colorado river near the Huasoroco mouth, 1957), which he calls closely related dialects of Mashco (the 2008 edition has 'Harakmbet' pencilled), about 75 known speakers; Glottolog lists Toyoeri and Sapiteri as dialects of Huachipaeri (huac1244). Only the footnote and the closing sentence of VII.A refer to Huachipaeri proper, via Pittman's unpublished analysis. The catalog entry is 'Huachipaeri' with no rule, so the Toyeri/Sapiteri statement is the closest available description and should be labelled by dialect.

readall_conflicts: Only one distinct work was readable (the two listed entries are the same Peck 1958/1979/2008 report; the MPG copy is access-restricted). Within Peck there is an internal tension worth recording: Peck's own statement for Toyeri/Sapiteri is penultimate stress with an antepenultimate exception class and lengthening of every stressed vowel, with stress, length and morpheme boundaries all flagged as 'unresolved' and no minimal pairs found; but he reports (p. 12 fn. 3, p. 27) that Pittman's unpublished analysis of Huachipaeri proper concluded vowel length is phonemic and stress is non-phonemic, predictable from vowel durations. If Pittman is right, the deeper generalisation for Huachipaeri proper would be a length-driven (weight-sensitive) placement rather than fixed penult, but Pittman's analysis is unpublished and only known through Peck, so fixed: penultimate syllable (with exceptions) is what the opened text supports.

audit.recode_to: Penultimate stress (default) within a morphologically delimited domain: certain final suffixes/syllables (-ta, -nda, -na, ne, -a 'et al.') fall outside it, giving surface antepenult — i.e. the same set by morphology/penult-in-stem-domain type already coded for amar1274, now on huac1244's own evidence (Peck 1979 [2008]: 27, Toyeri and Sapiteri dialects). Carry cautions: author calls the suprasegmentals 'no resueltos', verbs with suffix strings 'más compleja', all stressed vowels long and no stress minimal pairs; Pittman (unpublished, Huachipaeri proper) held stress non-phonemic and predictable from vowel length. strength of the evidence: primary preliminary phonology sketch (1956-57 fieldwork), not open-text/undetermined.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every fragment of the deciding Van linden 2023 quotation is verbatim in the postprint text we hold at the stated pages (3, 4, 7, 29). (2) Deciding source: a 2023 handbook sketch of the sister language Arakmbut (amar1274) that explicitly excludes Watipaeri; the record was left not determinable solely because the Huachipaeri-side primaries were unreachable on 12 Sep (an automated-access block on sil.org, PuRe 401, no the Internet Archive). Glottolog lists exactly two phonology items for huac1244: Peck 2008 [1979] (Glottolog's most extensive description, 104 pp) and van den Eynde 1972 (43 pp). (3) I located an open archive. VII.A 'Acento' p. 27 states penultimate stress in most polysyllables with antepenult in words

Peck gives a concrete default-penult rule (with extrametrical-like final syllables) for the Toyeri/Sapiteri varieties and reports Pittman's Huachipaeri finding (stress non-phonemic, predictable from vowel length). This is the same passage as the verified existing statement held by the project (reading 'fixed: penultimate syllable'), so it agrees with that statement and adds nothing new beyond it; no contradiction with the catalog, which…
